name: sealed-hierarchy-exhaustive-match
intent: Close a type hierarchy so the compiler knows every variant, and dispatch each operation through a match that it proves exhaustive - adding an operation never touches the variants, and adding a variant breaks every incomplete match at build time instead of at run time.
problem: A value hierarchy with a stable set of variants keeps needing new operations, but the hierarchy is open and dispatch is unchecked. Either every operation is written as a Visitor - an accept() method on each variant, a visitor interface with one method per variant, a class per operation - or as chains of type tests whose default arm silently swallows cases added later. Nothing separates 'everything is handled' from 'one case was forgotten', so completeness rests on review and tests. The decision is to declare the variant set closed where the compiler can see it (sealed/permits, enum, closed class, union, sealed trait, private constructors) and to express each operation as a total match over that set, so coverage becomes a compile-time fact and Visitor's double-dispatch machinery is not needed.
context: Applies to in-process hierarchies the team owns end to end: ASTs and IRs, domain events, commands and results, protocol frames, state machine states, status and error taxonomies. It presupposes a closure declaration the compiler can see in full (sealed/permits, enum, closed class, union, sealed trait, private constructors) plus a match construct it checks exhaustively (pattern switch, when, match, switch expression, visitation of a closed variant type), the whole set living in one compilation unit or assembly, and a build in which the coverage diagnostic is escalated to an error and catch-all arms are reserved for deliberate escapes. It is the wrong tool where variants are contributed across a published boundary or where the variant identity is data rather than a declaration.
benefits: Completeness is proved at build time: a missing arm fails compilation at every operation site, so a forgotten variant cannot slip through as a silent default value.
Operations get cheap: a new operation is one match in the module that needs it - no accept() hooks, no visitor interface, no class per operation.
Variants stay passive data, carrying no knowledge of the operations applied to them, which keeps them easy to construct, compare, serialize and test.
The compiler's non-exhaustiveness report doubles as the refactoring plan: adding or removing a variant yields an itemised list of the sites that have to decide about it.
Cross-variant operations become expressible: one match can treat several variants together, table-drive the cases or expose a total function, none of which single dispatch allows.
Dispatch costs a tag test or a jump table instead of a virtual call per operation, and a closed set gives optimisers and analysers complete knowledge of the alternatives.
tradeoffs: It inverts the expression problem rather than removing it: adding a variant now breaks every match site precisely because adding an operation became cheap - a good trade only if operations really change more often than variants.

Closure is a boundary commitment: the proof exists only where the compiler sees the whole set, so any hierarchy that another module, assembly, plugin or customer may extend cannot be sealed without giving the guarantee back.
A single catch-all arm disables the proof for all future variants, and catch-all arms are the path of least resistance, so the pattern's value depends on a lint or review rule that forbids them.
Coverage is usually a warning rather than an error (Scala E029, C# CS8509, GCC -Wswitch), so the guarantee only becomes load-bearing once warnings-as-errors is configured for the build.

Behaviour no longer lives with the data: each operation reproduces the traversal, and a wide hierarchy accumulates parallel matches (switch soup) whose shared structure must be extracted deliberately.

Sealing couples the hierarchy to one compilation unit or assembly and to its source: downstream code cannot complete the set, and tooling that subclasses the base (mocks, generators) must be reworked.

The guarantee is compile-time and per-artifact: an exhaustive match built against an older version of the set throws at run time when the hierarchy gained a case without the match site being rebuilt, so the hierarchy and its matches must ship together.

participants.responsibility: Names the complete set of alternatives where the compiler can see it - sealed/permits, enum, closed class, union, sealed trait, private constructor - and thereby fixes the boundary every coverage analysis reasons about.
One immutable alternative carrying its own payload; it exposes no operation method (no accept(), no visitX()) and therefore does not change when an operation is added.

A single match expression or statement over the closed set with one arm per variant: it holds the whole algorithm for one operation in one place and is rejected or flagged by the checker when an arm is missing.

The compiler's exhaustiveness analysis - or, in partially typed settings, the type checker or linter - that turns the closure declaration plus the match arms into a per-site completeness proof, typically surfaced as a diagnostic that CI escalates to an error.

The deliberate, documented opening of the set (wildcard/else/default arm, non-sealed, #[non_exhaustive], @unknown default); its presence is a boundary decision, and it means coverage no longer extends to future variants.

use_cases: Compiler front ends and IRs: one sealed node set with separate exhaustive matches for parsing, type checking, optimisation, evaluation and printing, replacing a visitor per pass.
Domain events and commands: a closed set of event records dispatched to projections, validators and notification builders, each match compiled against the complete set.
API and transport results: Ok | NotFound | Conflict | Invalid | Unexpected mapped in one total match per surface (HTTP status, CLI exit code, UI state) instead of scattered type tests.
State machines and lifecycle statuses: transition tables and state renderers written as matches over a closed state set, so a new state cannot be forgotten in one of them.
Wire protocols and file formats with a fixed message taxonomy decoded into a closed union, where every encoder, decoder and pretty-printer has to be total.

Refactoring an existing Visitor hierarchy once the team owns all element types: accept() methods and visitor interfaces collapse into sealed cases plus one match per operation (the standard Java 21 / Kotlin / Scala / C# migration).

Android UI layer: the official architecture guidance models ViewModel UI state as a Kotlin sealed type whose Loading/Success/Error variants are rendered through an exhaustive when, so adding a state breaks every screen that has not decided how to draw it.

Elm's Architecture: application messages are a closed union type and the compiler's completeness check rejects any update function missing a branch for a newly added Msg tag - exhaustiveness as the application's dispatch contract.

Deliberate openness inside a sealed platform: Swift Evolution SE-0192 freezes most enums but marks C-imported and resilient modules' enums non-frozen, where every switch over them must carry a (possibly @unknown) default - the escape hatch reserved exactly where future variants are planned.
avoid_when: The hierarchy is an extension point for other teams, plugins or customers: sealing forbids their types - stay with open polymorphism, or accept the open trade with Extensible Visitor, Acyclic Visitor or a dispatch table.
Variants are added far more often than operations: the cost of a variant is paid at every match site, so per-variant polymorphic methods localise that change much better.
The variant identity is data (plugin ids, dynamically registered types, user-defined tags): a dispatch table keyed by the tag is the right structure, not a compile-time closed set.

The set mirrors an external protocol that evolves independently: model the unknown case explicitly (an Unknown variant, @unknown default, #[non_exhaustive]) or keep a tolerant reader instead of pretending closure.
Only one or two trivial operations exist and the variants already own the behaviour: a virtual method or a Strategy object is less machinery than a sealed declaration plus a match.

The language cannot prove coverage and the build cannot afford a type checker (plain JavaScript, Ruby without Sorbet): a table-driven dispatch with a loudly failing default is more honest than a switch that only looks exhaustive.
anti_patterns: Writing a default/else/case _ arm 'to be safe': it compiles, silences the coverage check, and turns every variant added later into a silently wrong fallback.
Claiming closure by convention - package-private constructors, a naming discipline, a comment - in a language that checks nothing, then calling the dispatch exhaustive.
Keeping the visitor interfaces and accept() methods after dispatch moved into matches: two dispatch mechanisms for one hierarchy, both of which must be maintained and can disagree.

Sealing a type that was designed as an extension point (framework base classes, plugin interfaces) and reintroducing non-sealed or non_exhaustive later to undo it - the closure contract is added and revoked, and stops being trusted.

Duplicating the traversal skeleton in every operation (switch soup) instead of extracting the shared walk, so arm-local invariants drift apart and one new variant needs edits in several near-identical copies.
Modelling a genuinely open protocol as a sealed set with an Unknown(raw) case that every arm treats identically - a fake variant that pays closure's price without delivering its benefit.
design_principles: Say what you know: if the domain fixes the alternatives, express that completeness in the type system instead of leaving it in reviewers' heads.
Locality of behaviour: an operation belongs in one place, next to the data it consumes, rather than scattered across every variant by double dispatch.
Make change visible: closure converts 'someone added a variant' from a silent behaviour change into a compile-time checklist.
Separation of data and operations: variants model shape, matches model processing, and neither has to know the other's full surface.
Honest boundaries: where the set must stay open, model the unknown case explicitly instead of pretending the closure holds.
best_practices: Declare closure in the language's own construct (sealed/permits, closed, enum, sealed!) rather than in comments, and keep the whole set in the compilation unit where the checker can see it.
Omit the catch-all arm in operations that are meant to be total; where one is unavoidable, make it fail loudly (throw, panic, preconditionFailure) and mark it as the documented escape hatch.
Escalate the coverage diagnostic to an error in CI (warnings-as-errors, -Wswitch-enum, Scala -Werror, mypy exhaustive-match, IDE0072) so the proof cannot rot quietly.
Keep variants immutable and payload-complete, one data type per variant; a sealed set of mutable cases with nullable fields loses the modelling benefit that motivated the closure.
Extract shared traversal into helpers so match arms stay thin and a new variant does not force edits in duplicated code.
Treat a change to the set as an API change: rebuild every consumer together (the guarantee is compile-time), and version or explicitly open the set when consumers are outside your release train.
sources: Gavin Bierman, JEP 409: Sealed Classes (OpenJDK, Java SE 17, 2021) - restricting a hierarchy to a known set of subtypes so exhaustive analysis becomes possible.
Gavin Bierman, JEP 441: Pattern Matching for switch (OpenJDK, Java SE 21, 2023) - type coverage over a sealed hierarchy, removal of the default clause and the MatchException migration contract.

C# 15 closed hierarchies proposal (.NET 11): a closed class lets a consuming switch expression be exhaustive without a default arm - https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/proposals/csharp-15.0/closed-hierarchies

Weixin Zhang & Bruno C. d. S. Oliveira, Castor: Programming with Extensible Generative Visitors, Science of Computer Programming (2020) - sealed case classes give exhaustiveness while the Visitor pattern suffers from the Expression Problem (https://wxzh.github.io/papers/scp2020.pdf).

Android Developers, State holders and UI state and Recommendations for Views: UI state modelled as a Kotlin sealed type exhaustively handled in when expressions (https://developer.android.com/topic/architecture/ui-layer/stateholders, https://developer.android.com/topic/architecture/views/recommendations-views).

An Introduction to Elm, Custom Types: union types and the compiler's completeness check that forces every case of the Msg union to be handled in update (https://guide.elm-lang.org/types/custom_types.html).

The Swift Programming Language, Statements: switch must be exhaustive over the scrutinee's type, non-frozen enums require a (possibly @unknown) default; see Swift Evolution SE-0192 for the frozen/non-frozen boundary (https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/ReferenceManual/Statements.html, https://github.com/apple/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0192-non-exhaustive-enums.md).

Scala 3 reference, E029 Pattern Match Exhaustivity: the coverage diagnostic and its two sanctioned resolutions - add the missing case, or add a wildcard (https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/reference/error-codes/E029.html).

TypeScript Handbook, Narrowing: discriminated-union switches plus the never-typed exhaustiveness check that errors when a union member is unhandled (https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html).

Criticism of sealing by default: the extensibility and API-evolution case against closing a hierarchy unless the closure is a deliberate commitment (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6389417/should-i-recommend-sealing-classes-by-default; Dart's @sealed debate on sealing as a breaking change, https://github.com/dart-lang/sdk/issues/27372).
